cards.text: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, and he's still on the question of food sacrificed to idols. Now he writes one line twice: "Everything is permissible," and both times he hits the brakes. Both times, friend, there's a BUT coming.

cards.question: Paul writes "Everything is permissible," and then he hits the brakes. What does he add?
The second time around, Paul says that not everything that's permissible builds people up.

cards.text: Allowed and good for you are NOT the same thing. Just ask anybody who hit snooze SIX times and then ran into the boss in the hallway. So Paul tells them whose good they should really be chasing.

cards.question: Whose good does Paul tell the Corinthians to seek?

cards.text: Now Paul gets practical. First stop: the meat market, with somebody at the counter squinting at the meat like it owes them money, wondering where it's been.

cards.question: Somebody's buying meat at the market in Corinth. What does Paul tell them to do with anything sold there?

answers.text: Ask where it came from first
Skip all of it to be safe

cards.question: Paul backs that up with Scripture. The meat market is fine because the earth and its fullness belong to the ___.
Next scene: an unbeliever invites a believer to a meal, and the believer wants to go. Paul says to eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.

cards.text: But picture it: at that meal, somebody says, "This food was offered to idols," and the whole table goes QUIET. Forks frozen in midair like somebody hit pause on the whole dinner.

cards.question: Someone at the meal tells you the food was offered to idols. What does Paul say to do?
Paul says to skip that food for the sake of conscience. He means your own conscience.

cards.text: Then Paul asks why his freedom should be decided by someone else's conscience. And if he eats with thankfulness, why should he be denounced over the very thing he gave thanks for?

cards.question: Paul zooms ALL the way out. Whether you eat or drink, how much of life does he say should be done to the glory of God?

cards.text: Whatever you do means WHATEVER, friend. Snooze button included. Then Paul warns them not to become a stumbling block.

cards.question: Paul only warns against being a stumbling block to fellow believers.

cards.text: Then Paul points to himself. He tries to please everyone in all he does, and he's not after his own good but the good of many.

cards.question: Paul seeks the good of many, not his own, so that they may be ___.

cards.text: Paul ends with one line: "You are to imitate me," and then he says who HE imitates. If I told bakers to imitate me, friend, every one of you would end up face-first in the chocolate chips.

cards.question: Paul tells the Corinthians to imitate him, just as he imitates ___.

findings.problem: The setup rules out a wrong answer. Card 1 says 'there's a BUT coming,' and the question says Paul 'hits the brakes.' 'Everything is also helpful' is not a brake or a but, so the baker can drop it without knowing the passage.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences: 'Allowed and good for you are NOT the same thing.' / 'Just ask anybody who hit snooze...' / 'So Paul tells them...'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The question rules out the wrong answers. 'Paul zooms ALL the way out' and 'how much of life' signal the widest answer, so 'Only your mealtimes' and 'Only worship gatherings' are out before the baker reasons at all. The question also names eating and drinking, which undercuts 'Only your mealtimes.'

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences: 'Whatever you do means WHATEVER, friend.' / 'Snooze button included.' / 'Then Paul warns them...'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin talks to a group: 'If I told bakers to imitate me, friend, every one of you would end up face-first in the chocolate chips.' He should be talking to one baker.

rule.text: He calls the baker "baker" or "friend," and talks to one baker at a time. Never "my baker," "kids" or "sweetie."
